title: IQP Inspections for Access-Controlled Doors: The Compliance Check Most NZ Building Owners Overlook
description: Every access-controlled door in a New Zealand building with a compliance schedule carries a legal obligation under the Building Act — an annual inspection by an Independently Qualified Person, or IQP. The door must be inspected, tested, and reported to the local council each year, confirming it is performing to its specified standard. In practice, most building owners either do not know this applies to them, or they leave it until a compliance failure surfaces during a council audit. Red Wolf holds IQP qualifications and carries out these inspections as part of a broader access control service. We check that each door is latching, locking, and releasing correctly under all conditions — including alarm activation and power failure. If it is not performing to standard, we fix it and issue the required documentation. With the end of the calendar year approaching, now is a practical time to check whether your compliance schedule is current. If you are not sure whether your doors need an inspection, we can tell you in a short conversation what is required and what it will cost.

title: A New Study Found That Less Than Half of Organisations Are Confident in Their Active Assailant Response — Here Is What NZ Businesses Should Do About It
description: ASIS International and Everbridge released research this week showing that less than half of respondents are highly or mostly confident their staff know what to do in an active assailant incident. Four factors were linked to higher confidence: a comprehensive written plan, regular drills, communications technology, and a functioning behavioural threat assessment and management team. The gap between having a security system and having a prepared organisation is exactly what this finding describes. A camera at the front door and a monitored alarm panel do not tell your staff what to do when something happens. Physical security has two components — the technology layer and the human layer. Most businesses invest in the first and largely ignore the second. The organisations with the highest confidence in their readiness have both: documented procedures, tested regularly, supported by the right technology, and owned by someone with the authority to act. If your business has never run a scenario exercise or reviewed its emergency response documentation, that gap is worth closing before you need it.

title: 91% of Customer-Facing Workers Faced Aggression in the Past Year
description:
The NZSA signed the ShopCare Retail Pledge last week, formally recognising occupational violence and aggression as a critical risk in retail. The pledge follows the ShopCare National Customer Aggression Survey, which found that 91% of customer-facing workers experienced customer aggression in the past year.

That number changes how retail and hospitality operators across Auckland and Wellington should think about physical security. Aggression is not only a guarding problem. Site design and technology decide how quickly staff can get help and how well an incident is documented. Several controls reduce exposure:

• Duress buttons that reach a monitored response
• Clear camera coverage at counters and exits
• Intercom-controlled back-of-house doors
• Access control that stops an aggressor following staff into a secure area

In the same week, ASIS International released its revised Workplace Violence Prevention and Intervention Standard. It is an ANSI-approved framework for evaluating a programme, assigning clear roles and sustaining improvement. Pairing a framework like that with the right physical controls is where most NZ businesses still have room to improve.

If your team deals with the public, send us a message to book a review of how your site supports staff when an incident starts.

title: AI-Augmented Attacks Are Reaching Building Systems: What Johnson Controls Recommends
description:
Johnson Controls published a white paper last week on AI-augmented attacks. It covers what these attacks mean for operational technology, meaning the controllers and networks that run building systems, and how a zero-trust overlay can protect them.

This is where our Johnson Controls partnership matters. In large New Zealand facilities, access control, CCTV, intruder alarms and building management increasingly share networks. The older devices on those networks were rarely designed with modern attack methods in mind. Replacing every legacy controller is not realistic for most hospitals, campuses or commercial towers. A zero-trust overlay instead treats each device and connection as untrusted until verified, which limits how far an attacker can move once inside. The partnership gives our engineers access to enterprise-grade technology and guidance at that scale. Our job is to apply it to the specific mix of systems on a Wellington or Auckland site without disrupting day-to-day operations.

If your security and building systems share infrastructure and you're unsure how exposed the older devices are, reach out. We can talk through where to start.

title: What ISO 45001 Means When Our Technicians Work on Your Site
description:
Facilities managers running occupied buildings in Wellington and Auckland often give us the same brief: upgrade the security system without putting tenants, staff or the public at risk while the work happens. A typical security install involves ceiling access, live electrical work and working at height. In a hospital, school or busy office, the margin for error is small.

Red Wolf works under an ISO 45001 occupational health and safety management system, so site safety is planned, not improvised. Before work starts, we identify the hazards for that specific building and document them in a site-specific plan. Technicians follow agreed controls for isolation, working at height and keeping the public separated from the work area. We record and review incidents and near misses so the system keeps improving.

Under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, client and contractor share overlapping duties. A certified system gives your own health and safety team documented evidence that the contractor's risks are being managed. The outcome is an install your people barely notice, backed by a paper trail that stands up to scrutiny.

If you're planning security works in an occupied building, send us a message. We'll share how we would plan the job safely.

title: Eight Weeks Left in 2026: Which Security Gap Will You Close?
description:
Last week we published the results of our poll on the biggest physical security gap in NZ businesses. The takeaway stuck with us: you can't fix the gaps you haven't found. With roughly eight weeks left in 2026, that's the question worth asking before the year closes.

A year-end security review doesn't need to be a major project. A few checks cover most of it:

• Who still holds active credentials after a year of staff changes?
• Were the alarm and camera faults logged during the year actually resolved?
• Have the site layout, tenancy or operating hours changed since the system was designed?

Many Wellington and Auckland businesses also slow down over the Christmas and New Year break. Sites sit quieter and less supervised for weeks at a time, which is exactly when an unnoticed gap gets tested. Our position is simple: a short review now costs far less than finding the problem in January.
